video_title: Fall Market Swoon, Followed By An End-Of-Year Boom? | Mark Newton @Fundstrat_Direct
gist: Fundstrat technical strategist Mark Newton raises his year-end S&P 500 target to 8,000 (from 7,300) but expects a choppy, volatile stretch through the midterms driven by rising long-term yields, a crude oil bounce, and tech/semiconductor consolidation, while flagging a newly-announced Treasury duration-swap ('Treasury put') as a major cross-asset catalyst and favoring healthcare/biotech, energy, materials, precious metals and crypto over bonds and real estate in the interim.

insights.claim: Mark Newton raised his year-end S&P 500 price target to 8,000 from a prior 7,300, still expecting a positive close for the year.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A raised year-end target from a widely-followed technical strategist signals continued upside despite near-term chop; watch if he revises it again as September volatility plays out.
insights.quote: my target it was lifted to 8,000 from 7,300.

insights.claim: Newton expects the next two to three months (especially September) to be choppy and volatile before the market resumes its climb toward 8,000 by year-end, with the path unlikely to be a straight shot in either direction between mid-August and mid-November.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Investors should expect drawdowns/chop into the midterms rather than treat the current all-time-high breakout as a smooth continuation.

insights.claim: The March 2026 lows (final week of March) marked a bottom after which market breadth improved meaningfully, with financials, healthcare, discretionary and industrials all showing strong outperformance that cushioned the market while technology underwent a necessary consolidation.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Broadening participation beyond mega-cap tech is a structurally bullish signal for market resilience, reducing single-sector concentration risk.

insights.claim: The market traded sideways from May through mid-July 2026 before breaking out to new all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Confirms the consolidation-then-breakout pattern Newton uses to justify continued trend-following into new highs.

insights.claim: Newton views technology (about 30% of the market) as the single biggest tangible downside risk to the rally: a sharp tech nosedive is the one scenario that would clearly hurt the broader stock market, though he doesn't expect it to happen.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Position sizing in mega-cap tech/semis should account for concentration risk even amid a bullish overall call.
insights.quote: technology being 30% of the market if tech were to start to nose dive that is the absolute number one tangible point

insights.claim: Parts of tech, specifically semiconductors and memory names, still need to stabilize/consolidate before they can resume their prior momentum, similar to what software stocks went through earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Tactical investors should expect chip/memory names to lag near-term and look for a stabilization signal before adding.

insights.claim: AI and AI-adjacent companies make up roughly 45% of the S&P 500's total market cap and over 70% of the Nasdaq-100's market cap.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: This level of concentration means broad-index returns are now effectively a leveraged bet on AI capex and earnings delivering — a key risk to monitor for diversification purposes.
insights.quote: I've heard that AI and a AI adjacent companies make up more like 45% of the S&P's total market cap and like over 70% of the NASDAQ 100s.

insights.claim: The net return on AI capex is a major unresolved variable for markets: some companies report compute costs rising faster than productivity gains, which could force downward revisions to the AI-driven earnings estimates currently supporting valuations if returns don't show up soon.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Watch corporate commentary on AI ROI closely — a shift from 'transformative' to 'cost overrun' narratives would be an early warning for an earnings-estimate reset across ~45% of S&P market cap.

insights.claim: Newton stays bullish on the AI trend on pure trend-following grounds (his 'Newtonian inertia' framework: a trend in motion stays in motion until proven otherwise), and argues seeing potential bubble risk is different from having actual evidence to act on it.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A disciplined trend-follower's playbook: stay long AI exposure until technical trend evidence (not just valuation worry) breaks down, then react quickly.

insights.claim: Newton watches AI-linked bond issuance and IPO activity as leading indicators — he expects clear advance warning signals (not an overnight switch-off) when the AI investment cycle starts to slow.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Track AI-related debt issuance and IPO pipeline health as a real-time gauge for when to de-risk tech exposure.

insights.claim: Dramatic price increases from memory chip makers raise the risk that the government could eventually intervene on monopoly/antitrust grounds.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk is an underpriced tail risk for memory/semiconductor names benefiting from AI-driven pricing power.

themes.theme: The Treasury Put and Fed Dynamics

insights.claim: The US Treasury announced a duration swap — issuing more short-term bills to fund a dramatically expanded program of long-bond purchases — which effectively creates a 'Treasury put' that likely prevents 10-year yields from rising much above 4.75% and 30-year yields much above 5.30% without triggering intervention.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A de facto yield cap changes the risk/reward for long-duration bonds and rate-sensitive equities; a break above ~4.75%/10yr or ~5.30%/30yr would be a signal the put is being tested.
insights.quote: it creates, you know, a Treasury put where um, you know, yields likely cannot get too far above 475 on the 10-year

insights.claim: This is a sharp reversal from Treasury's stance just weeks earlier when officials said they intended to curb long-bond buying; they have now set plans to more than double it, which Newton calls a 'gamechanger' for rates markets.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A sudden policy U-turn of this size signals officials see real stress building in the long end of the curve — worth watching for further escalation.

insights.claim: Newton frames the Treasury's move as more like the 1961 Operation Twist than the 2011-2012 Fed twist, and expects it to be a source of reflation that lets the economy 'run hot' for a couple of years while neither political party addresses the need to cut spending.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A reflationary policy bias favors hard assets and real yields declining, reinforcing Newton's precious metals/commodities call.

insights.claim: Drawing on Lacy Hunt's read, Adam suggests Fed governor Worsh is likely frustrated by the Treasury's move because it undercuts his stated goal of the Fed stepping back so the market can send an unfiltered signal, since the Treasury just put its own thumb on that signal.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Tension between Fed communication policy and Treasury market intervention could create policy confusion that increases bond volatility.

insights.claim: Newton clarifies he is talking about long-term yields, not a Fed funds rate hike, and expects Fed governor Worsh to stay largely silent on markets at Jackson Hole rather than offer dovish forward guidance, despite the Treasury's move arguably giving him room to sound more dovish.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Don't expect a dovish Fed pivot signal from Jackson Hole even as the Treasury moves to cap yields — the two policy levers are moving somewhat independently right now.

insights.claim: Inflation breakeven expectations have been 'nosediving,' and recent CPI/PCE/GDP data have reinforced rather than undermined the Fed's inaction, despite widespread expectations that tariffs and other factors would prove more inflationary.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Soft breakevens argue against an inflation scare derailing the bull case near-term, supporting Newton's view that any current inflation stickiness is temporary.

insights.claim: Newton believes the dollar's decline this week (versus the yen) is one of the most important market moves of the last month and signals the start of a broader multi-year dollar downtrend, even if dollar/yen bounces after the yen reaches roughly 151.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A structural dollar downtrend is a tradeable multi-year macro call with knock-on effects for commodities, EM assets, and multinational earnings.
insights.quote: My my thinking is the dollar's move this week is probably one of the more important moves of the last month.

insights.claim: A weaker dollar would benefit US earnings because roughly 40% of aggregate US company revenue comes from overseas, and many US entities effectively hold assets in foreign currencies while liabilities are dollar-denominated.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A declining dollar is a tailwind for large-cap multinational earnings and a reason not to fight the 'weak dollar as a feature, not a bug' policy bias.
insights.quote: we know that 40% of most companies revenues come from overseas.

insights.claim: Crude oil is likely to continue its bounce that began in July, pushing higher into mid-September/early October, which Newton flags as a likely source of market discomfort.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A rising oil price into fall is one of Newton's top three near-term risk catalysts for equity volatility alongside tech consolidation and rising yields.

insights.claim: GCC oil producers are already rerouting pipelines through the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman at a rapid pace to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz following the recent regional conflict, a structural shift rather than a temporary reaction.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Structurally lower reliance on the Strait reduces the market's sensitivity to Middle East chokepoint risk over time — a slow-moving but important geopolitical de-risking trend for energy investors.

insights.claim: The US itself is not dependent on the Strait of Hormuz (unlike the rest of the world), and Newton expects US net oil exports to rise materially as the world reroutes away from the Strait, reinforcing the US position in global energy.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Rising US net energy exports is a structural positive for the dollar's reserve role and US energy-sector earnings even as the broader dollar trend weakens.
insights.quote: US actually isn't dependent on the straight but the rest of the world is

themes.theme: Fiscal Debt, Politics and the Midterms

insights.claim: US federal debt crossed $40 trillion this month with the annual deficit running over $2 trillion, even during what Newton calls a 'Goldilocks' economic period — raising the question of what happens to the deficit in a downturn.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Structural deficits growing even in good times is a long-horizon risk factor for real yields, the dollar, and fiscal-dominance dynamics that could resurface once growth slows.
insights.quote: We just hit 40 trillion this month which is a mindbogglingly large number. Um the deficit is over two trillion.

insights.claim: Newton compares current Fed/Treasury tools for managing debt to the post-WWII period, when US debt-to-GDP fell from about 110% to 40% over three decades via yield-curve-style suppression; Adam pushes back that this is an imperfect ('apples to oranges') comparison since the postwar US benefited from being the world's rebuilding manufacturing hub and didn't carry today's structural deficit and entitlement burden.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The WWII debt-reduction playbook may not replicate today given different structural growth drivers — investors shouldn't assume yield suppression alone resolves the debt problem this time.
insights.quote: we did the same thing during World War II, 1946. the debt to GDP was about 110% maybe and they took that down to 40% in about three decades

insights.claim: Newton references Treasury Secretary Bessent's '3-3-3' fiscal framework — targeting a 3% deficit-to-GDP ratio and roughly 3 million additional barrels of oil production per day — as evidence of an active policy roadmap, though he couldn't recall the plan's third component.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: The 3-3-3 plan is a concrete policy benchmark to track for evidence the administration is following through on fiscal consolidation goals.
insights.quote: Scott's initial 333 program you know GDP uh debt to GDP of 3% of GDP deficit uh what do you say 3 million barrels of oil a day

insights.claim: Markets tend to embrace political gridlock, and with the GOP's slim congressional margins likely to keep governance divided even if Democrats retake the House, Newton doesn't expect the midterm outcome to meaningfully change market-relevant policy either way.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Don't over-position around midterm election outcomes — Newton's framework says continued gridlock is the base case and is historically bullish for stocks.
insights.quote: markets tend to embrace um gridlock

insights.claim: Newton expects partisanship to ease somewhat after the midterms regardless of outcome, potentially clearing the path for stalled bipartisan legislation like the Clarity Act to pass, and historically midterm-year weakness into October/November has been one of the best buying windows in the four-year political cycle.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A seasonal/political framework for timing adds: treat pre-midterm October/November weakness as a historically favorable entry window rather than a reason to de-risk further.

insights.claim: Newton's near-term tactical favorites are healthcare/biotech (citing GLP-1 drug momentum after the sector was under pressure since 2023), energy, materials, and precious and base metals, while he'd keep long-term technology holdings rather than sell into consolidation.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A concrete sector rotation playbook for the next few months: overweight healthcare/biotech, energy, materials and metals; hold (don't chase) tech through its consolidation.
insights.quote: I would invest in uh healthcare. I I respect the momentum of what's going on with the GLP-1 drugs and and some of the what's happening in biotechnology

insights.claim: Gold, silver and crypto bottomed on their monthly cycles in summer and have just begun a fresh leg higher; Newton expects a consolidation phase from late August into September before further gains, recommending investors buy dips in both metals and crypto through that window.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A near-term pullback in metals/crypto should be treated as a buying opportunity rather than a trend change, per Newton's cycle work.

insights.claim: Newton expects technology to become tactically buyable again by around the midterm elections once semiconductor/memory names stabilize, framing current tech weakness as a long-term-trend-intact dip rather than a reversal.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Sets a rough timing marker (post-midterms) for re-adding tactical tech exposure.

insights.claim: Rising long-term yields make bonds and rate-sensitive real estate vulnerable near-term, with 30-year mortgage rates already around 6.7% pressuring the housing market.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Underweight duration and rate-sensitive real estate exposure while the Treasury's long-end yield picture remains unsettled.

insights.claim: Real estate performance is highly localized: within the Reno metro area some submarkets are projected for price increases while nearby pockets face declines, and parts of Florida have already been pulling back sharply in recent months.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: National real estate narratives are unreliable; investors need submarket-level data before acting on housing exposure.

insights.claim: Newton flags a roughly 18.5-year long-term real estate cycle that appears to be peaking now, with a cycle bottom expected around 2029; he personally sold his home (which carried a roughly 3% mortgage) to sit on the sidelines of a potential downturn and redeployed that capital into AI stocks.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A well-known technical cycle (the ~18-year real estate cycle) is being used by a professional strategist to justify exiting owned real estate now in favor of AI equity exposure — a notable real-money positioning signal.
insights.quote: I had a mortgage at right around 3% and I sold my home and very happy to just be on the sidelines there and sort of waiting for the crash so to speak and investing my money in AI stocks

themes.theme: Macro Cycle, Growth and Confirming Signals

insights.claim: Corporate profit growth is running at its highest level in roughly 30 years, which Newton treats as the single biggest offsetting factor against debt, rate, and geopolitical concerns for the stock market's medium-term path.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: As long as this earnings strength persists, Newton argues it outweighs macro risk factors — a reason to stay long despite headline debt/rate worries; watch for any rollover in profit growth as a trend-change signal.
insights.quote: earnings are literally the highest we've seen in about 30 years with regards to profit growth

insights.claim: US quarterly GDP growth has decelerated sharply over the past year: 3.8% (Q2 2025), 4.4% (Q3 2025), 0.5% (Q4 2025, partly tariff-related), 2.1% (Q1 2026), and 1.5% (Q2 2026) — a declining trend that Adam flags as a risk but Newton is not concerned about for 2026 or 2027.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A visibly decelerating GDP trend sitting underneath strong equity markets and elevated AI-driven profit growth is a divergence worth tracking for signs it eventually catches up with earnings.

insights.claim: Newton's cycle work points to a bullish window through roughly Q3 2028, after which his cycles turn down into 2030 — meaning he sees no recession-level concern in 2026 or 2027 specifically.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Gives a multi-year time horizon for the bull case to play out before Newton's own framework flags real downside risk — useful for setting a portfolio review checkpoint around 2028.

insights.claim: High-yield credit markets are currently showing no signs of stress, and Newton treats housing as the likely 'first shoe to drop' if rising long-term rates were to actually damage the economy.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Two concrete tripwires to monitor for a genuine economic-risk regime change: high-yield spread widening and housing-market deterioration, rather than headline debt/deficit numbers.

insights.claim: Current market sentiment is mixed rather than extreme in either direction, which Newton reads as healthy; lingering investor concern is keeping many people underinvested even as the technical and earnings picture stays constructive.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: Non-extreme sentiment plus underinvestment is typically a supportive backdrop for further gains rather than a contrarian sell signal.

insights.claim: Newton's core methodology is to respect the prevailing trend and use technical signals to strip emotion out of decisions, while reacting early once there is actual trend-reversal evidence rather than waiting for full confirmation that a bubble has burst.
insights.speaker: Mark Newton
insights.so_what: A repeatable risk-management rule for any asset (AI stocks included): don't front-run a trend reversal on valuation worry alone, but be ready to exit quickly once the trend itself breaks.
